rationale: The open premise of the AddVoter finding was whether the staging description is the contract or stale text, and the captured membership design document settles most of it: it is not a stray code comment but the repository's own membership proposal, which defines Staging, lists 'AddVoter: server becomes staging unless voter' among the client operations, draws the nonvoter -> staging -> voter transition, and - in the same document - defers the promotion algorithm to a later change. That splits the account: the absent promotion loop is a declared gap rather than a new defect, while the suffrage decision (the new server is a voter at once) contradicts what the document lists, and the deprecation notes in configuration.go show the maintainers may have settled on immediate addition with AddNonvoter as the replacement. This submission corrects the account and the knowledge entry it rests on, with the affected uses named, rather than leaving the wider reading in place.

knowledge.changed_premise: The contract source named in the original statement was the AddVoter doc comment alone. The captured membership.md is also a contract source that lists AddVoter as making the server staging, and the same document defers the promotion algorithm, so the statement now distinguishes the suffrage decision (which the code contradicts) from the promotion loop (which the document itself declares unimplemented). The behaviour described is unchanged: the configuration change installs the server as a Voter in one step and nothing creates a Staging server.
knowledge.statement: The AddVoter configuration change installs the requested server with Suffrage Voter in one step: nextConfiguration's AddVoter branch builds the new Server with Suffrage Voter, the resulting configuration is appended as a single LogConfiguration (or the deprecated remove-peer entry below protocol version 2), and the leader applies it to the commitment and to replication immediately after dispatching it. No captured path creates a Staging server or defers promotion, so the suffrage the operation installs contradicts both published descriptions of the operation (the AddVoter doc comment and membership.md, which lists 'AddVoter: server becomes staging unless voter'), while the promotion loop that membership.md describes is separately declared unimplemented in that same document. The code also deprecates the Staging suffrage and notes that the old AddStaging command was in fact AddVoter, and the Promote command can only act on a Staging server, which no path creates.
knowledge.conditions: Protocol version 2 or above for the ID-based API; the cluster has a leader able to commit the configuration entry; the requested server may be absent from the cluster entirely (a fresh ID and address).

interpretations.rationale: Corrected account with the membership document in hand; the three declared comparisons and their witnesses are unchanged from the previous revision (added server appears as a Voter on indices 1 and 5; single-voter cluster loses its leader, its applies answer not-leader and its removal answers not-leader, on indices 2 and 3; the three-voter control keeps working on indices 6 and 7). What changes is the contract side and the scope of the claim. membership.md is a design proposal in the repository that defines Staging and the nonvoter -> staging -> voter transition, lists 'AddVoter: server becomes staging unless voter' among the client operations, and in the same document defers the promotion algorithm to a separate change; the AddVoter doc comment repeats the staging promise. So the missing promotion loop is not a new defect - the document itself declares it unimplemented - while the suffrage the operation installs is a direct contradiction of what the document lists, and it is the half with the consequence this run measured: on a single-voter cluster the newly installed voter is immediately part of the quorum, the leader's lease check then finds fewer voters than the quorum, and the cluster is left with no leader, no commits and no way to remove the entry through the API. The behavioural claim therefore survives, narrowed to the suffrage decision and to callers who follow either published description, with the promotion loop explicitly outside it.
counterevidence: The document is phrased as a proposal ('We propose to re-define...'), and configuration.go deprecates the Staging suffrage and notes that the old AddStaging command was in fact AddVoter while Promote can only act on a Staging server that nothing creates; under that reading the maintainers deliberately settled on immediate voter addition with AddNonvoter as the staging replacement, the implementation is intended, and what is defective is that two published descriptions still promise staging - a documentation divergence rather than an implementation error.
Adding a voter that is not running is a membership mistake in Raft terms; the harm here is that the published descriptions license that workflow by promising a staging step before voting rights.

Recovery is possible out of band through RecoverCluster, with its documented warning that it implicitly commits the log, so the accurate statement is that no in-band repair exists rather than that the cluster is unrecoverable.

The consequence needs the quorum relation: for one added server it is specific to a single-voter cluster, and the three-voter control in this run shows the same operation is harmless when the living voters still meet the quorum.
limitations: Two shapes were probed (one and three living voters, one added server each); the general condition is the quorum exceeding the living voters, which the probe brackets rather than enumerates.
The added server is never started, so no promotion behaviour can be observed - and per the same document no promotion path is implemented to observe.

The probe runs one process with the in-memory transport, so a real deployment would show a client timing out rather than the ErrNotLeader answer recorded here; that difference is inferred from the API's error semantics rather than observed.

Which side of the divergence the maintainers consider authoritative is not decided here; the account states what the code does, what the published descriptions say, and the measured consequence of following them.
